newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Higher airfares could result from emergency talks.
newsitem.headline: Higher airfares could result from emergency talks.

text.p: Delegates from the world's airlines begin a round of emergency meetings in Geneva on Wednesday to discuss strategies to counter a recent surge in fuel prices that is gnawing at their profitability.

The industry's global body, the International Air Transport Association (IATA), said last week at its annual general meeting that airlines were on course for their second consecutive year of record profits.

But a rise in jet fuel prices of around 30 percent on the back of higher crude oil prices in recent months has forced IATA to retreat from its April forecast for an industrywide profit of about $6 billion this year.

IATA director-general Pierre Jeanniot said at the meeting that the group now expected a net result for its more than 250 members, which represent 98 per cent of international scheduled flights, of about $5.5 billion.

A number of airlines -- among the latest Hong Kong's Cathay Pacific and Dubai's Emirates Airline on Tuesday -- have added surcharges to their cargo rates in recent weeks and some airline executives want higher passenger fares as well.
Scandinavian airline SAS took this route on Tuesday, announcing passenger ticket increases of two per cent -- combined with a cargo rate increase of five per cent -- effective from Friday.
British Airways last week reported a 2.1 percent drop in its first half operating profits compared to a year ago.

But BA said strong traffic growth and greater productivity would have boosted profits by 10.5 percent had it not been for an extra 51 million pounds ($84 million) spent on its fuel bills together with the impact of a threatened pilots strike in July.

"It's reasonably serious. Fuel is between eight and 10 percent of costs and prices have gone up by 30 percent or more, so overall costs are up three percent," said Barclays de Zoete Wedd airline analyst Nick Cunningham.
The emergency meeting is the first to be called IATA since 1991 when the airlines were suffering the throes of the fuel price gyrations caused by the Gulf War.

Airlines paid an average worldwide price last year of 65.2 U.S. cents a gallon (4.5 litres). But the price soared to 77.5 cents in September after the United States fired 27 cruise missiles against Iraq as a warning to Baghdad to comply with Gulf War ceasefire resolutions.
Delegates will gather in Geneva on Wednesday and the meetings are expected to last through Friday.

IATA officials say that up to a maximum 106 of its 254 members traditionally take part in the so-called tariff coordination meetings. The delegates will spend much of the time assessing the situation airline by airline.
Decisions open to them include raising fares across the board or on a select number of routes or simply levy surcharges on some or all of the routes, an IATA spokesman said.
Lufthansa AG chairman Juergen Weber said at the IATA general meeting last week that higher fuel prices had cost his airline around 100 million marks ($67 million) in added expense in recent months.
Other companies, such as Japan Airlines, have not yet decided policy on surcharges for passengers and cargo.
But BZW's Cunningham pointed out that even if the airlines did decide to increase passenger fares there was no guarantee that the problem would be solved.
"The question is A: will the customer tolerate them and B: will the airlines hold ranks," Cunningham said.

He said BA has been pushing up fares in business and first class to test market acceptance. But airlines on the continent -- Lufthansa, KLM and Air France in particular -- have been competing aggressively.
"So it should be difficult to put three percent back on prices ... they could put on three percent, but carry on discounting," Cunningham added. ($1=.6050 Pound, $1=1.4945 Mark)
